title: Address ingress wavefronts and continuous-batcher skew causing cross-tenant queue starvation
creator: Laura Chen
description:
Summary: Multiple customers across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments reported sudden latency regressions and request timeouts during short-spike ingress patterns. Root cause analysis points to an interaction between the continuous-batcher admission watermarking and recent KV-cache eviction heuristics which allows 'wavefront' microbursts to monopolize admission, starving heterogeneous long-context flows and amplifying long-context tail latency.

Scope: Incidents observed in production for 3 customers (two Hosted, one Dedicated enterprise) and reproduced in a Private deployment lab. Affects mixed-length workloads where short requests arrive in tight bursts followed by scattered long-context requests.

Observed symptoms:
- Small requests processed quickly but cause admission reservoir to saturate for several batching windows, preventing long-context requests from entering batches.
- Long-context requests queue for multiple batch cycles, accumulating KV-cache misses and inflating token generation latency (long-context tail).
- In Dedicated capacity, autoscaler thresholds cause reactive scaling which further shifts admission priorities, worsening starvation.

Initial hypothesis: Recent admission watermark optimization intended to improve CPU/GPU utilization favors minimal-latency short batches by lowering admission thresholds when backlog is low. Under wavefront microbursts this heuristic fails to account for pending long-context tickets, causing starvation. Additionally, KV-cache eviction now favors aggressive size-based eviction, making long-context requests suffer cache thrash when finally scheduled.

Immediate mitigation applied (hotfix):
- Reverted watermark aggressiveness for admission logic on prod clusters serving mixed-length workloads.
- Introduced short-term admission guard: if any request in waiting queue has expected tokens > 2048, reserve at least one slot in the upcoming batch window for heavy requests.
- Rolled back the most aggressive KV-cache eviction patch on Dedicated clusters with confirmed incidents.

Longer-term fix plan (this ticket):
1) Implement 'reservation windows' within the continuous-batcher to guarantee minimal representation of long-context flows during microburst events.
2) Add admission fairness metrics and a per-tenant histogram for pending expected-token distribution.
3) Adjust KV-cache eviction hysteresis to be workload-aware (prefer eviction of small-context entries first during contention windows).
4) Add automated canary that replays mixed-length synthetic traffic to detect starvation regressions before deploy.

Acceptance criteria:
- No reproduced starvation in the lab for 1M mixed-length synthetic requests replayed across variable microburst patterns.
- Production rollout shows 90th and 99th percentile tail latency for long-context requests reduced to baseline (pre-regression) within two rollout stages.
- No increase in small-request P99 latency >10% during rollout.

Monitoring & metrics to track:
- Admission window fairness ratio (short:long served per window).
- Queue wait time distribution by expected token length.
- KV-cache hit/miss ratio correlated with wait time.
- Customer-facing error rates and 95/99/99.9 latency buckets for affected routes.

Rollout strategy:
- Canary on a single low-traffic Hosted region for 24h.
- If metrics stable, expand to remaining Hosted regions and one Dedicated pool.
- Finally, stage rollout to Private customers with opt-in and provide transitional config toggle.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for admission reservation logic and eviction hysteresis.
- End-to-end integration test using workload-generator harness (conforms to documented production mix).
- Load test at 2x peak observed traffic to verify no regression in throughput.

Stakeholders and comms:

- Customer success contacts: Priya Nair, Omar Velasquez

Notes: This ticket bundles a customer-facing hotfix and the engineering work to harden admission fairness. Work must coordinate with Dedicated autoscaling engineers to avoid adverse coupling between admission heuristics and scale-up events.
